title: Trump Admits Calling Netanyahu 'Crazy' Amid Stalled Iran Peace Talks
summary: President Donald Trump acknowledged Wednesday that he called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 'crazy' during a phone call, saying he was 'a little bit perturbed' that Israel's ongoing conflict with Hezbollah in Lebanon was holding back peace negotiations with Iran. In an interview with The New York Post's 'Pod Force One,' Trump insisted his relationship with Netanyahu remains solid. 'We've worked very well together. I like Bibi a lot,' he said, using Netanyahu's nickname. Netanyahu, speaking on CNBC, responded that the two leaders sometimes have 'tactical disagreements' but share 'common goals' and 'agree on the main things.' The candid remarks highlight the growing pressure Trump faces to resolve the Iran war, now in its fourth month, as rising energy prices and economic uncertainty threaten Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Talks have dragged on for weeks as mediators try to extend a fragile ceasefire into a more enduring truce. The negotiations are further strained by Israel's broadening war with the Iranian-backed Hezbollah militia in Lebanon. Iran insists any potential truce must also quell the fighting in Lebanon. Trump remained noncommittal about a timeline, suggesting the Strait of Hormuz—a crucial oil shipping route—might stay blocked through Labor Day. He added that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his late father, is 'involved' in peace talks but is not doing well due to wounds from an airstrike. The violence continues to escalate. On Wednesday, Iranian drones hit a passenger terminal at Kuwait's main airport, killing one person and wounding dozens. Hours later, an Israeli strike hit a car on a busy highway south of Beirut, just before a second day of U.S.-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel in Washington. The strike came without warning, and it was unclear if the target was killed. The attacks test a nominal ceasefire that has been in effect since April 17, with both sides accusing each other of violations. The path to a lasting peace remains deeply uncertain.
why_it_matters: Instability in the Middle East can spike energy prices, impacting family budgets and the global economy; the war demonstrates how personal diplomacy and regional conflicts can quickly escalate, affecting students' futures in a connected world. The outcome may determine whether teens face high gas prices and economic uncertainty in their early adulthood.

questions.question: Since when has a nominal ceasefire been in effect?

background_read: The Iran war, now in its fourth month, began after tensions over Iran's nuclear program escalated, drawing in US forces. The Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of the world's oil passes, is a chokepoint that when blocked can cause energy prices to surge, a major worry ahead of the US midterm elections in November. Israel has a long history of conflict with Hezbollah, an Iranian-backed Shia militia in Lebanon, including a devastating 2006 war. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, has at times clashed with US presidents while maintaining close security ties. Iran's new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, assumed power after his father's death but is seen as less experienced, and the airstrike injuries he reportedly suffered add further uncertainty to the peace talks. The nominal ceasefire that has been in place since April 17 has been repeatedly violated, illustrating the fragility of such agreements in a multiparty conflict.

perspectives.description: The candid exchange may clear the air and allow both leaders to negotiate more honestly, potentially accelerating a peace deal that would lower energy prices and reduce violence.
The personal insults risk damaging the long-standing U.S.-Israel alliance and may encourage Iran to harden its stance, prolonging a war that kills civilians and destabilizes the region.

History shows that U.S. presidents have often used both public praise and private pressure with Israeli leaders; the outcome depends on whether tactical disagreements can be resolved without undermining the broader strategic partnership.

If the ceasefire holds and expands, diplomatic channels could lead to a broader Middle East peace framework; if it collapses, the U.S. might face difficult choices ahead of a volatile election season.
